---
title: "What it might mean for the parser to (not) be the grammar"
subtitle: "Is a grammar an abstraction over the parser, or an information resource the parser consults?"
author:
  - tim-hunter
date: "2026-11-12"
categories: [parsing, grammar]
---


Suppose it's agreed that the following system of phrase-structure rules accurately 
characterizes the sentences that a certain group of speakers recognize as well-formed 
sentences of their language (and the structures that they associate with those sentences):

    S → NP VP       NP → it
    NP → D N        D → the
    VP → V NP       D → a
                    N → cat
                    N → dog
                    V → chased
                    V → watched

What are the ways in which this collection of rules might relate the actual work 
that speakers do in the course of recognizing and understanding sentences? There are 
at least two possibilities.

The first possibility is that these rules are a sort of compact, abstract description 
of the workings of the sentence-processing mechanism. That sentence-processing mechanism 
works in some particular more-or-less incremental manner, and it would be perfectly 
possible to accurately describe the workings of this mechanism without appealing at 
all to the particular level of abstraction that these rules live at. Researchers might 
find it helpful to write rules in the form above for certain purposes, as a kind of 
summary of what is possible given the workings of this particular processing mechanism, 
but it is those workings that are primary. This is approximately the view that is sometimes 
put in slogan form as "the parser is the grammar", since on this view the parser and 
the grammar are not really two different things, but rather two different ways of looking 
at a single thing. Let's call this the **grammar-as-abstraction** view.

The second possibility is that the rules above are mentally represented in their own 
right, and this system of rules is one of the pieces of information that is consulted by 
the sentence-processing mechanism in the course of understanding a sentence. On this 
view the rules themselves are primary, and they inform the workings of the processing 
mechanism. Let's call this the **grammar-as-information** view.

I'm not going to try to review previous debates about these two views, but I think many 
readers will recognize that both views are out there, and that discussions about the 
interplay between our best grammatical theories and work in sentence processing 
sometimes get muddied because of vagueness, inconsistencies or disagreements between 
these two views.

My goal here is to put forward a way of thinking about this question that makes things a 
little bit more concrete (perhaps this is not the only way to make things concrete, but 
it's at least one way), so as to identify some of the kinds of empirical evidence that 
could be brought to bear on the question. This will lead to what I think is some 
suggestive evidence in favor of the grammar-as-information view; unsurprisingly, there 
will be plenty of scope for objections along the way, and I don't expect the argument 
to be convincing to everyone, but I hope that the argument form itself is at least 
interesting and perhaps could clarify the nature of the questions at hand.

It will be useful to first consider a very simple system of sentence recognition, the 
shift-reduce recognizer, before turning to the one where I think things actually get 
interesting, which is the left-corner recognizer.

## Shift-reduce recognition

Let's consider one particular way in which sentence recognition could proceed in accord 
with the phrase-structure rules given above (where "in accord with" is deliberately 
agnostic, for now, about the distinction between grammar-as-abstraction and 
grammar-as-information): shift-reduce recognition.

There are two kinds of moves, or transitions, that this simple kind of processor can make. 
A `shift` transition consumes a word of input and pushes the word's category onto the stack 
that comprises the processor's memory. A `reduce` transition replaces two adjacent symbols 
on the top of the stack, each of which represents the category of some constituent that 
has been found, with another symbol representing the category of their parent constituent.

Here's how this kind of processor would recognize the sentence `the dog chased it`.

|       |           | Rule          | Position              | Stack contents    |
| ---   | ---       | ---           | ---                   | ---               |
| 0     |           |               | • the dog chased it   |                   |
| 1     | shift     | D → the       | the • dog chased it   | D                 |
| 2     | shift     | N → dog       | the dog • chased it   | D N               |
| 3     | reduce    | NP → D N      | the dog • chased it   | NP                |
| 4     | shift     | V → chased    | the dog chased • it   | NP V              |
| 5     | shift     | NP → it       | the dog chased it •   | NP V NP           |
| 6     | reduce    | VP → V NP     | the dog chased it •   | NP VP             |
| 7     | reduce    | S → NP VP     | the dog chased it •   | S                 |

Suppose we have determined that the sequence of steps shown in this table is an accurate 
characterization of the steps that are carried out in the relevant speakers' minds in 
the course of comprehending that sentence. We can then consider 
the different ways of thinking about grammatical rules: in each line of the table above, 
what is the relationship between the rule listed in the third column and the 
stack-manipulation that happens in the fifth column?

According to the grammar-as-abstraction view, the processor has transitions available to it 
that manipulate the stack in certain ways -- for example, it can consume the word `dog` and 
push `N` onto the stack, and it can replace a `V NP` sequence at the top of the stack with a `VP` 
-- and those stack-manipulating transitions are, in a sense, "all there is". Writing things 
like `VP → V NP` in the third column is a helpful way for us to encapsulate certain aspects 
of what's going on (and writing out the full rule list at the beginning of this post is a 
helpful way to summarize the overall capacity of this processing device), but no more than 
that.

According to the grammar-as-information view, on the other hand, the rules are more 
fundamental than the stack manipulations. On this view there is a mental list of rules which 
is consulted, and the fact that the processor finds `VP → V NP` in that list is what "tells it" 
that it can replace `V NP` with `VP`. On each line of the table, the rule in the third column 
is what the processor has looked at in order to determine that the stack manipulations in 
the fifth column are licensed. The processor, on this view, is something that takes in two 
different kinds of information, a collection of grammar rules and a sequence of words, and 
tries to knit them together in a certain way.

In this particular case of a simple shift-reduce processor, I think it is **very** difficult 
to tell these two views apart. This is because there is a one-to-one correspondence between 
processing transitions and grammar rules. For every `shift` transition that the grammar-as-abstraction 
proponent posits as part of the processor, there is exactly one rule of the form `X → blah` that 
the grammar-as-information proponent posits on the list of rules; and for every `reduce` transition, 
there is exactly one rule of the form `X → Y Z`. Knowing that the relevant mental processing 
proceeds as in the table above seems equally compatible with either of these views.

If this was the situation we were in regarding human sentence processing, perhaps one could 
argue that, in the absence of positive evidence for the kind of separation that the 
grammar-as-information view posits, the grammar-as-abstraction view should be preferred on 
the grounds of simplicity; or, perhaps one could argue that, because of the one-to-one 
correspondence between transitions and rules, the supposed distinction between the two views 
turns out to be misguided, and the question is moot. But this is probably not actually the situation 
we find ourselves in when it comes to human sentence processing: the relevant mechanisms there 
are, to the best of our knowledge, more complicated than the simple shift-reduce system, and 
more complicated in ways that allow for the distinction between the two views to come more 
clearly into focus.

## Left-corner recognition

Things get more interesting when we turn to left-corner recognition. The fundamental difference 
compared to shift-reduce recognition is that the processor is able to represent a certain 
kind of incomplete constituents. More specifically, the stack maintained by a left-corner 
recognizer contains not just symbols like `NP` and `VP` representing constituents that have been 
completely identified, but also symbols of the form `X/Y` (e.g. `NP/N` or `S/VP`) which represent 
an `X` that is missing a `Y` on its right edge.

Here are the steps by which a left-corner recognizer would process the same sentence from before.

|       |           | Rule          | Position              | Stack contents    |
| ---   | ---       | ---           | ---                   | ---               |
| 0     |           |               | • the dog chased it   |                   |
| 1     | shift     | D → the       | the • dog chased it   | D                 |
| 2     | project   | NP → D N      | the • dog chased it   | NP/N              |
| 3     | match     | N → dog       | the dog • chased it   | NP                |
| 4     | project   | S → NP VP     | the dog • chased it   | S/VP              |
| 5     | shift     | V → chased    | the dog chased • it   | S/VP V            |
| 6     | complete  | VP → V NP     | the dog chased • it   | S/NP              |
| 7     | match     | NP → it       | the dog chased it •   | S                 |

To clarify the meaning of the `X/Y` notation, here are pictures representing the first three 
steps.

<image width="500" src="https://gist.githubusercontent.com/timhunter/f7efd9a0b144cedb6b17fec9231c9bc5/raw/left-corner-step1-step2-step3.png">

Unlike the shift-reduce system, where the `NP` constituent is posited only after **both** of 
its daughter constituents are identified, here the `NP` constituent is posited at Step 2, 
when only its left daughter has been identified; the transitions of this form are called 
`project` transitions. Of course the fact that the right daughter hasn't yet been found needs 
to be tracked, which is why after Step 2 we have `NP/N` on the stack rather than simply `NP`. 
At Step 3 the processor consumes the next word, `dog`, which allows it to "pay off the debt" 
and arrive at a full `NP`; this kind of debt-repayment transition is called a `match` 
transition (since it "matches" the owed category against the incoming word).

The `project` transition at Step 4 introduces the `S` constituent, on the basis of having found 
its left daughter, in the same way that the one at Step 2 introduced the `NP` constituent. 
Notice that at Step 5, the incoming word `chased` cannot itself pay off the owed `VP`, so this 
is not a `match` transition like the one at Step 3, but rather is a `shift` transition (like 
the one at Step 1) which adds to the stack, specifically it introduces a `V`.

The next transition is where things get particularly interesting.

<image width="500" src="https://gist.githubusercontent.com/timhunter/f7efd9a0b144cedb6b17fec9231c9bc5/raw/left-corner-step5-step6.png">

The transition at Step 6 is different from any of the three kinds of transitions we have 
seen before (`shift`, `project` and `match`). It has something in common with the `project` transitions 
that we saw at Step 2 and Step 4: it involves positing a `VP` on the basis of its left daughter 
(a `V`), and taking on a debt of the right daughter (an `NP`). But instead of this posited parent 
constituent being freshly introduced to the stack, like the `NP` at Step 2 or the `S` at Step 4, 
this posited parent is used to pay off the owed `VP`. The newly-owed `NP` becomes all that is 
missing from the `S` constituent, hence we have simply `S/NP`. 
This kind of transition is called a `complete` transition. 
The final `match` transition at Step 7 fills in the missing `NP` (in just the same way that the 
match transition at Step 3 filled in a missing `N`).

What I take to be significant here is that, unlike in the simple shift-reduce system, there is 
no one-to-one correspondence between grammatical rules and stack-manipulating transitions: 
for each grammatical rule of the form `X → ...`, the processor has one transition that introduces 
a new (possibly incomplete) `X`, and one transition that pays off an owed `X`. 
For rules of the form `X → blah`, this is the distinction between what `shift` and `match` (both of 
which consume `blah` from the input) do with `X`. For rules of the form `X → Y Z`, this is the distinction 
between what `project` and `complete` (both of which build on a `Y` and take on an owed `Z`) do with `X`.

<image width="800" src="https://gist.githubusercontent.com/timhunter/f7efd9a0b144cedb6b17fec9231c9bc5/raw/left-corner-schemas.png">

## So what?

It's quite easy to make sense of this under the grammar-as-information view. The processor itself 
"knows" only the four schemas or templates illustrated above (one each for `shift`, `match`, `project` 
and `complete`), and consults the list of grammatical rules to determine how those schemas can be 
instantiated. The transition at Step 2 above arose from instantiating the `project` schema using 
the rule `NP → D N`, and the transition at Step 6 arose from instantiating the `complete` schema 
using the rule `VP → V NP`.

In the example above, we don't see any single grammatical rule being used by two distinct 
schemas, but if we modify the sentence very slightly we can see what this would look like: 
if the sentence were `the dog chased the cat`, then the first six steps would proceed as above, and 
then at Step 8 we see a `complete` step that makes use of the same `NP → D N` rule that was used to 
instantiate the `project` schema at Step 2.

|       |           | Rule          | Position                  | Stack contents    |
| ---   | ---       | ---           | ---                       | ---               |
| ...   | ...       | ...           | ...                       | ...               |
| 6     | complete  | VP → V NP     | the dog chased • the cat  | S/NP              |
| 7     | shift     | D → the       | the dog chased the • cat  | S/NP D            |
| 8     | complete  | NP → D N      | the dog chased the • cat  | S/N               |
| 9     | match     | N → cat       | the dog chased the cat •  | S                 |

So the rule `NP → D N` can be used to instantiate the `project` schema to yield a transition 
that replaces `D` with `NP/N`, and can also be used to instantiate the `complete` schema to yield 
a transition that replaces `⋯/NP D` with `⋯/N`.

More generally, given some list of rules, each one is going to be instantiable via two schemas 
(either by `shift` and by `match`, or by `project` and by `complete`), and thus will give rise to two 
possible transitions. If there are, say, 10 rules in the grammar, the four schemas above will 
give rise to 20 possible transitions.

This makes things start to look strange under the grammar-as-abstraction view. If the 
stack-manipulating transitions are primitive, rather than derived by instantiating schemas, 
then there is no particular reason to think that these transitions should come in the neat 
pairs that they seem to. It would look like a coincidence if, for every transition that 
replaces `Y` with `X/Z`, there's always another transition that replaces `⋯/X Y` with 
`⋯/Z`. If the transition that replaces `D` with `NP/N` and the transition that replaces 
`⋯/NP D` with `⋯/N` are just two of the 20 primitive transitions, then "the next 
language over" might have just one of these two; this would mean that the constituents that 
could appear as an `NP` in a subject position would differ from those that could appear as an 
`NP` in an object position, for example. To the extent that the next language over always 
corresponds to what we would get by making some change to the underlying list of rules and 
letting the transition schemas work with that modified list -- for example, if the next 
language over lacks both the `D` to `NP/N` stack transition and the `⋯/NP D` to `⋯/N` 
stack transition -- it makes less sense to think of the transitions themselves as primitive.

Notice how this is different from the situation with shift-reduce recognition, where there's 
a one-to-one correspondence between rules and transitions. If the only consequence of having 
`NP → D N` in your list of rules is the possibility of stack transitions that replace `D N` with 
`NP`, then it matters less whether you think of the rule or the transition as primitive. From 
a grammar-as-information perspective, the next language over might lack the `NP → D N` rule, 
and therefore the processor won't have available the move of replacing `D N` with `NP`; this is 
about the same as the prediction we'd make from a grammar-as-abstraction perspective, where 
the next language over just lacks the primitive stack transition that replaces `D N` with `NP`.

Another way to make the point is to observe that, if I tell you that the tree diagram for a 
certain sentence includes an `NP` node with a `D` left daughter and an `N` right daughter, you know 
that the shift-reduce recognition of this sentence will necessarily involve a step of 
replacing `D N` with `NP`. But we can't say (without knowing more about the position of the `NP` 
node) whether the left-corner recognition of this sentence will involve a step of replacing 
`D` with `NP/N`, or a step of replacing `⋯/NP D` with `⋯/N`. This one-to-many (specifically, 
one-to-two) relationship between the rules and transitions is what provides the impetus for 
treating a rule itself as a meaningful primitive, something that can be separated from any 
**single** action that might take place in the course of processing a sentence.

## The bigger picture

The main suggestion I want to put on the table is that this kind of one-to-many relationship 
between grammar rules and parser actions is a key form of evidence that might be used in support 
of the grammar-as-information view. One might agree that this is an interesting form of argument 
that could in principle be used to in support of the grammar-as-information view, without buying 
into any claims that the specifics of human sentence processing look anything like the picture 
I laid out with left-corner recognition above.

Having said that, there's some reason to think that human processing does in fact proceed in 
something along the lines of the left-corner manner outlined above. The evidence is based on 
the fact that the amount of memory (stack space) required by the left-corner recognizer gets 
large for center-embedded sentences, but not for left-embedded or right-embedded sentences, 
and therefore aligns neatly with the pattern of difficulty that humans experience with these 
constructions ([Resnik 1992](https://aclanthology.org/C92-1032/), and many references there). 
And as Resnik points out in that paper (section 4), it's particularly critical that when a 
posited parent node is going to "pay off a debt", this must happen as soon as the parent is 
posited; in other words, it's critical that we have `complete` as a separate transition schema 
from `project`, which is what leads to the one-to-many relationship between rules and transitions. 
(The alternative "arc-standard" system where rules of the form `X → Y Z` are **only** associated 
with `project` transitions, and there's a separate operation that "cancels out" parents posited 
by `project` with owed categories, does not yield the same predictions about memory load.)

Of course, a full-fledged theory of human sentence processing is going to look different in 
the details, not least because the relevant notion of syntactic structure-building is likely 
to have more bells and whistles than the simple trees that are describable via phrase-structure 
rules of the sort used above. If the processing system needs to deal with those additional 
bells and whistles, is it likely that things will fall neatly into place with a one-to-one 
correspondence between rules (of a new enriched sort) and transitions, like in the shift-reduce 
system, or it is more likely that things will get yet more complicated and diverge even 
further from such a one-to-one correspondence? It doesn't seem crazy to lean slightly towards 
the latter, all else being equal. And for what it's worth, although I'm not suggesting that 
this should hold much water, this seems to be what we see in parsers that extend the 
left-corner system illustrated above to incorporate movement 
([Stanojević and Stabler 2018](https://aclanthology.org/W18-2809/), 
 [Hunter et al. 2019](https://aclanthology.org/W19-2901/)): 
the point in the above was that the parser needs to treat merge steps that create left 
daughters differently from those that create right daughters, and once movement is introduced 
it becomes similarly necessary to distinguish typical, simple movement dependencies from 
those that have been derived via remnant movement.
